ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study was approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board (IRB), Michael C. Frank, Principal Investigator.

The pilot study, to determine the developmental appropriateness of the measures, as well as to enable final item selection, was conducted in the fall of 2025, using Prolific, an online research platform, to recruit, manage, and compensate participants.
Potential participants were identified as adults with children 28 to 50 months of age who currently reside in primarily English-speaking homes in the US.
Participants were first asked to provide informed consent with a waiver of documentation and to complete basic demographic and health questions.
Upon completion of the CDI-IIIR, participants were redirected back to Prolific where they received a payment of $6.
This led us to inviting child language researchers to use the CDI-IIIR on Web-CDI, as well as using Prolific for recruitment.
These participants were all recruited through Prolific.
We are close to having exhausted recruitment through Prolific for our inclusion criteria, and are seeking to obtain additional data through ongoing research projects.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Development and psychometric properties of the CDI-IIIR for language assessment of 30-to 48-month-olds

author.affiliation: University of New Mexico Northwestern University Arizona State University

text.text: The Macarthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDI) are a set of widely used parentreport instruments for measuring young children's language development.
The most widely used measures for English-speaking children are the CDIs for 8-30 months.
There is a strong need for both clinical and research purpose for comparable measures for three-year-olds.
The previously published U.S. English CDI-III yielded norms for 30-37 months only, due to ceiling effects, and assessed limited aspects of language.
Recent adaptations for Swedish and other Scandinavian languages, have used a different design and showed strong psychometric properties for children 2.5-4 years old.

The current study utilizes insights from that work to revise the CDI-III for an expanded target age range, and to incorporate more aspects of language, including morphology and metalinguistic and print awareness.

Results are presented for a sample of 202 children as reported on a pilot version of the new instrument, for both the full set of items and those items selected on the basis of IRT analysis for the final instrument, and also for a preliminary norming sample of 322 children utilizing the final instrument.
The CDI-IIIR appears to have good reliability and developmental sensitivity across the target age range of 30 through 48 months.
A larger norming sample, and validation evidence, are essential next steps.

Parent report instruments, such as the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDIs), have proven to be highly useful measures of young children's language and communicative development (Marchman & Dale, 2023).
text.formatted: Parent report instruments, such as the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDIs), have proven to be highly useful measures of young children's language and communicative development (Marchman & Dale, 2023).

text.text: Parents tend to be keen observers of their children and can provide valid reports of their behaviors, especially in a recognition rather than recall format, that are based on extensive observation over many contexts, rather than the brief and limited observation possible in a research or clinic visit.
The breadth of observation also reduces biases due to the variable frequency of use of words and specific structures, particularly omission of low-frequency items in brief samples.
Consequently, these instruments are well suited for capturing the range of children's language knowledge and use, which benefits from observation across diverse interactional contexts.
In addition, parental (or other caregiver) questionnaires do not require a trained clinician or researcher, making them a costeffective option for assessment.
For these reasons, parent report measures make possible research and norming studies with far larger samples than methods that require a trained researcher or clinician and child cooperation.

Indeed, the two original versions of the CDIs -the Words and Gestures (CDI:WG), for children 8-18 months, and the Words and Sentences (CDI:WS), for children 16-30 months -have grown widely in use over the last twenty years, including adaptation into over 100 languages (Laudańska et al., 2026;   Marchman & Dale, 2023;Weisleder et al., 2024).

text.text: However, the need for a parent report instrument that captures the language development of English-speaking three-year-olds has largely been left unmet.
Here, we describe the development of a revised version of the CDI-III, the CDI-IIIR, aimed at English-speaking children from 30 to 48 months.

The original CDIs focused on capturing children's language and communication in the first and second years, enabling users to track the emergence of language, the vocabulary explosion, and the beginnings of grammar (Fenson et al., 1994; Frank et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The original CDIs focused on capturing children's language and communication in the first and second years, enabling users to track the emergence of language, the vocabulary explosion, and the beginnings of grammar <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fenson et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Frank et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The success of these CDIs naturally gave rise to a desire for a comparable instrument that worked beyond the age of 30 months, when children enter a more advanced stage of language development.

During the third and fourth years, children continue to exhibit growth in vocabulary, with the noticeable addition of more abstract words, including a larger number of verbs and adjectives, and nouns that describe less observable concepts such as feelings and mental states (Clark, 1993; Dunn et al., 1987; Gleitman et al., 2005).

text.text: There are also tremendous advances in morphology and syntax during this period, as children use more inflectional forms and start to produce sentences with multiple clauses (Bloom et al., 1980; Bowerman, 1979; Vasilyeva et al., 2008).

text.text: Children's pronunciation tends to become clearer and more intelligible after age 3, and some three-yearolds exhibit skills associated with early literacy, such as noticing words that rhyme or identifying their initial sound (Anthony & Francis, 2005; Hustad et al., 2020).

text.text: In sum, there are many advances in children's language use at this age that are desirable to capture.
Assessment in this age range is also important for practical reasons.

Measures of language at or after 3 years of age have been shown to be better predictors of later language and literacy abilities than measures taken at earlier ages (Flax et al., 2009; Hammer et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2020; Lee, 2010).

text.text: Hence, they are especially appropriate for measuring the effects of early experiences, such as preterm birth or exposure to environmental toxins, and for recommending specialized speech and language services to those who are not meeting the expected benchmarks (Bishop et al., 2016).

text.text: In the United States, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) Part B, mandates that schools provide appropriate services for children between 3 and 5 years of age who have developmental delays, creating a need for effective tools to evaluate language delays in preschool children.

However, there are few parent report instruments to assess language and communication in English-speaking children 3-4 years of age, and those that do exist have significant limitations (see Table 1; see also (Feltner et al., 2024).

text.text: For example, the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ (Bricker et al., 1999) is a developmental screener for children 4 to 60 months that is commonly used in pediatric settings, yet it includes only a broad, 5-7 question assessment of children's communication, without detailed information about vocabulary, morphosyntax, or other areas of language.

text.text: In contrast, the Developmental Vocabulary Assessment for Parents (DVAP, (Libertus et al., 2013)) focuses exclusively on vocabulary (and in fact is heavily based on nouns, verbs and adjectives that are easily picturable, as it is based on the PPVT word list), and the Intelligibility in Context Scale (ICS (McLeod et al., 2012)) focuses exclusively on pronunciation/intelligibility, each leaving out key areas of language development.

Thus, most existing parent report instruments are either too broad or too narrow, in scope and/or age range, to fulfill the need for a language assessment for English-speaking preschool children (see Figure 1).

text.text: The CDI-III contains a 100-item vocabulary checklist, a 12-item syntax scale developed from the complexity measure in CDI-W&S, and a third section with 12 items reflecting language use in a broad sense.

text.text: Studies using the CDI-III have shown it has high internal consistency and concurrent validity with the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test-Revised, the McCarthy Scales of Children's Abilities, and the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (Feldman et al., 2005; Mercure, 1999; Oliver et al., 2002; Perra et al., 2015).

text.text: Thus, the CDI-III addresses many of the needs identified above: it has all the advantages of parent-report instruments, including ease of use in large-scale projects, measures several areas of language relevant to this age range, and has strong internal and external validity.
However, a major limitation of the CDI-III is a substantial ceiling effect, especially in the domain of vocabulary.

Therefore, although originally intended for children up to age 4, norms were developed and published only for children between 30 and 37 months (Fenson et al., 2007), significantly limiting its potential use.

text.text: Over the last decade, the CDI-III has been adapted to several other languages with greater success in covering a broader age range.

There have been two main paths taken to develop these adaptations (see Šmit Brleković & Kuvač Kraljević, 2023, for an overview).

The emphasis has been on finding individual words appropriately difficult for the target age range.

The Basque adaptation of the CDI-III, the KGNZ-3, for example, was extensively adapted and modified to reflect both the cultural context and structure of this non-Indo-European language (Ezeizabarrena et al., 2013).

text.text: Here, the vocabulary list focuses on four specific semantic categories: food-related words, body-related words, cognitive words and emotion words.

These categories were selected based on evidence that they are developmentally appropriate, show substantial growth during the target age range, and relate to themes that are central in the lives of most children.
To evaluate morphology and grammar, a section of 10 items asks about the child's use of complex phrases and another section of eight items queries the child's use of grammatical markers.

A section of seven items on metalinguistic awareness asks caregivers to comment on their child's phonological and orthographic awareness as well as their awareness of the existence of other languages.
Finally, one question asks about children's pronunciation/intelligibility.
This version was normed on a nationally representative Swedish sample for children up to 48 months of age, very substantially reducing the ceiling effect observed in the original CDI III.
Several other adaptations have since followed the Swedish model, both with respect to the structure of the vocabulary checklist and the incorporation of scales for additional aspects of language.

They include those for Norwegian (Holm et al., 2023), Finnish (Stolt, 2023), European Portuguese (Cadime et al., 2021), Croatian (Šmit Brleković & Kuvač Kraljević, 2023), Estonian (Tulviste & Schults, 2020), and Slovenian (Penko et al., 2026).

text.text: This research thus provides overall evidence that the Swedish CDI-III offers a useful model of a CDI for this age range.

The purpose of the current project was to take advantage of the successful work done in other languages to revise the CDI-III to achieve two aims: (1) expand the useable target age range, and (2) incorporate more aspects of language.
The revision leaned most heavily on the model used for the Swedish CDI-III and other Scandinavian forms, given their success.
The present paper describes the development of the revised CDI-III, the CDI-IIIR, and reports on a pilot study to evaluate its psychometric properties.
A working group was convened for the development of a revised CDI-III, to be titled the CDI- The largest and most central component, as usual for early language measures, was Vocabulary.
In the Swedish and other recent versions, there were four subcategories: Food-related words; Body-related words; Words about thinking; and Words about feeling.

The present working group wished to include a new category of time-, space-and quantity-related words, so Words about thinking and Words about feeling were combined into a single category, and the new category served as the fourth.
However, these categories primarily served to help parents recall related words.
Norms for the individual vocabulary categories were not developed in this project, or in most other CDI-III projects.
The working group then contacted five researchers (see Acknowledgements) with extensive experience in early language assessment to review this first version, and a number of changes were made.
The final pilot version is available upon request to the first author of this paper.

Final item selection was predominantly based on IRT analysis for each scale.
A two-parameter (2PL) model was identified as the most appropriate.

Item decisions were based primarily on the goals of maximizing the uniformity of distribution of item difficulty to ensure sensitivity at the extremes, and within that framework, maximizing item discrimination.
We also tried to minimize potential ambiguity to parents as well as items with excessive cultural specificity.

These additional issues beyond IRT parameters led to replacement for about 10 of the items initially selected based on the statistics alone, generally using the item with next highest item discrimination in that difficulty category.

On the basis of the preceding, largely positive results from the pilot study and selection of final items, we have begun the norming study for the CDI-IIIR.
For measures in the fourth year of life, twomonth age windows are typical and will probably be used in final norming results.
For the period 30-48 months, this would entail 9 such windows plus a one-month window.
Assuming a target of 40 children of each sex for each age category, this would require a total of 800 children, although more would be better.
Also highly desirable would be a norming sample less skewed toward higher maternal education/SES than in the pilot study, and more ethnically diverse.
This led us to inviting child language researchers to use the CDI-IIIR on Web-CDI, as well as using Prolific for recruitment.

Announcements were made on info-childes and other email lists (e.g., the Cognitive Development Society), and at the Symposium on Research in Child Language Disorders (SRCLD), informing researchers of the availability of the CDI-IIIR, and offering the use of Web-CDI for administration and scoring at no charge in exchange for sharing of anonymized data.
As of 5/3/2026, we have completed the initial phase of collecting a norming sample of language assessment of children between 30 and 48 months inclusive.
(Note the restriction to the actual target range for the instrument in these analyses.)
These participants were all recruited through Prolific.
We are close to having exhausted recruitment through Prolific for our inclusion criteria, and are seeking to obtain additional data through ongoing research projects.

For sample description in this preliminary report, actual age in months (rather than two-month age categories) will be used. 408 parents of children in this age range began the questionnaire, but 55 did not complete it, resulting in an initial sample of data for 370 children, of whom 194 are female, 174 are male, and 2 for whom parents chose not to report.
Maternal education was relatively high in this sample, as expected; median education was 16 years, and only 14.9% had 12 years or less of education.

As is typical for CDI measures, reliability is a major strength.

Internal consistency was excellent for Vocabulary (α = .98-.99) and good for Grammar and Sentence Complexity (α = .87-.95), comparable to the corresponding scales on the original CDI-III (Marchman et al., 2023).

text.text: The two brief metalinguistic scales were less reliable (Talking about Language α = .70-.78; Talking about Print α = .64-.70) and are best regarded as short indicators of an emerging domain.

These properties were essentially unchanged when IRT-based item selection reduced the pilot item set by roughly half, indicating that the final, shorter form retains the measurement characteristics of the pilot version.

Sex and socioeconomic effects were small and in line with prior CDI work: a female advantage reached significance only for Vocabulary (about 2% of age-residualized variance), and maternal education was reliably related only to Sentence Complexity (about 2%), an association likely attenuated by the restricted range of maternal education in these samples.
The pilot pronunciation items neither cohered nor tracked age and were dropped as a scale, though two global intelligibility questions were retained for their clinical utility.

There were also substantial intercorrelations among the subscales, with strong correlations between the three oral language scales (Vocabulary, Grammar, and Sentence Complexity) and weaker to non-significant correlations between the oral language and the metalinguistic scales.

This pattern is consistent with what has been reported for other CDI-IIIs, which report strong intercorrelations between most of the subsections except for pronunciation and metalinguistics (Holm et al., 2023; Brieković & Kraljević, 2023; Tulviste & Shults, 2020).

The somewhat smaller age effects for the CDI-IIIR are not unexpected: U.S. samples typically show greater variability in health, environmental exposures, and access to services than the more homogeneous European samples on which these adaptations were normed (e.g., Bradbury et al., 2015).

text.text: Several steps remain essential before the value of the CDI-IIIR for research and clinical work can be confirmed.
For norming, a larger and more representative sample is needed, particularly with respect to sex and ethnicity.

Following the approach used for the CDI: Words & Gestures and CDI: Words & Sentences norms (Marchman et al., 2023), it is highly desirable to have enough representation across maternal education and race/ethnicity to permit weighting, so that population parameters can be estimated more accurately relative to the U.S. population.

text.text: Validation studies are equally important: concurrent validity against other language measures for this age range -both structured assessments and language-sample measures -and longitudinal studies relating CDI-IIIR scores to earlier and later CDI scores.

Finally, the sensitivity and specificity of the CDI-IIIR for identifying language delay relative to established clinical measures will matter greatly to many users; we have already received several expressions of interest in carrying out such research.

It included the authors of the present paper and two additional graduate students, Matthew Betashour and Natalie Rossman.

On the basis of a review of other CDI-III instruments, it was decided to largely follow the design of Eriksson's Swedish version, with six components (eventual target number of items and actual number in the pilot version in parentheses): General Level of Communication (1,1); Expressive Vocabulary (100, 210); Grammar/Morphology (10,17); Sentence Complexity (10,18); Pronunciation (5,6); and Talking about Language and Print (15,10).
Later it was decided to divide this last component into two components: Talking about Language (6), and Talking about Print (4).

The working group reviewed the items in several other CDI-III adaptations for appropriate items, as well as drawing on their own experience and knowledge of the literature, in order to create the pilot version.
